summary:
Tucumán stands under Argentina's national framework, and no Tucumán-specific rule material enough to depart from it is sourced here. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012, permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, so an adult visitor's identity documents are not gated by medical sign-off. The statute remains on the books.

That statutory position has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal. A decree issued on 5 February 2025 restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the minors' measure illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

Official hostility at national level is documented. The government of President Javier Milei eliminated the federal Ministry of Women, Gender and Diversity and dismissed trans employees hired under the Trans Labour Quota Law, which reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs for trans people. Argentine trans activists interviewed on 4 April 2025 described the community as facing a chaotic and desperate situation, with heightened exposure to violence, discrimination and poverty.

Violence risk is the sharper practical concern for a visitor. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, a record and a rate of one every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims (142 cases); 18 victims were trans men against 5 in 2024, 13 were lesbians and 4 were non-binary people. Some 64.8% of cases (147) involved physical violence, 32% occurred inside police stations or penal institutions, and recorded police involvement rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, which raises the practical risk attached to any contact with law enforcement.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, but rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance removed by an appeal court in 2020, so the gender-motivated aggravator does not apply in the case as it now stands.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina was the first country in the region to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws. An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration across the framework a visitor enters.

The 2025 violence figures extend a trend rather than an isolated spike: trans men victims rose from 5 in 2024 to 18 in 2025, and police involvement in recorded hate-crime cases moved from 17 to 64 over the same period, while total cases set a record. Agencia Presentes reported the figures on 19 March 2026 and described them as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.

The United Nations described Law 26.743 as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region when it was passed by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention. Trans activists in Buenos Aires, including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán, stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins, told the Washington Blade on 4 April 2025 that the national government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence.
localsOnly:
Residents face the loss of institutional machinery that had served them. The federal Ministry of Women, Gender and Diversity has been eliminated, and trans public servants hired under the Trans Labour Quota Law, which reserved at least 1% of public-sector positions for trans people, were dismissed, removing both a policy voice and a statutory employment channel.

The decree of 5 February 2025 governs residents rather than visitors directly, restricting minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy, and a second decree regulates where transgender prisoners are housed. Legal experts who called the minors' decree illegal and unconstitutional signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention, and residents remain subject to it while that challenge is unresolved.

Hate-crime monitoring records the burden falling on residents: trans women and travestis made up 62.5% of the 227 bias-motivated crimes logged in 2025, and 32% of all cases took place in police stations or penal institutions. National and provincial anti-discrimination laws supply the protection machinery residents can invoke, alongside the 2012 Gender Identity Law.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the litigation against the February 2025 decree on gender-affirming care for minors is unresolved in the sources available here, so the decree's current operative status cannot be confirmed.

No Tucumán-specific statute, provincial decree or administrative practice on legal gender markers, facilities access, or provincial care provision is sourced here; the province is treated as standing wholly under the national framework. Whether Tucumán has its own hate-crime reporting channel or provincial breakdown of the national figures is not sourced.

Nationally, whether the travesticidio aggravating circumstance will be applied in any future proceeding beyond the Sacayán case, and whether the 2025 record in hate-crime figures changes legislative responses, remain unresolved here. Access to gender-affirming care for adult visitors in Tucumán, and any waiting lists or provider availability, is not sourced.
